lignes.texte: 13.8 billion years ago, the universe exploded out of a single, infinitesimal point.
It’s a great story… and it’s impossible. The point of singularity isn’t a real
place. It’s a glitch. A cosmic error code where physics and gravity broke down.
Now deep space exploration is exposing the cracks at the foundation of
cosmology. And it’s shattering reality. If the Bang wasn’t the beginning… what
really happened at the start of the universe? For generations, Albert Einstein’s General
Theory of Relativity, told us that the history of the universe could be traced back in a simple
straight line. The further back you go, the closer the stars and galaxies and atoms get,
until, eventually everything is condensed into a tiny and dense point.
Time Zero. There’s just one problem.
At Time Zero the laws of physics and time die. Einstein proved that space and time aren’t
separate. They form a 4 dimensional fabric called space-time. Mass bends
it and gravity shapes it. But when you compress it all into a single location,
the idea of a continuous fabric falls apart. There’s no logical way to explain it.
At that point, quantum physics takes over. But General Relativity ignores quantum mechanics.
Condensing classical gravity all the way to zero volume forces the universe’s ultimation
to divide by zero… a mathematical impossibility. The textbook explanation of how the universe
formed, the idea of a “birth from nothing”, isn’t an established fact.
It’s a theory riddled with holes. Scientists have desperately tried
to paper over those holes with different ideas and theories over the years. Arguably the most
famous and widely-accepted of those theories is the “Lambda Cold Dark Matter” model. It
tries to explain how the universe started, how it grew, and how it continues to expand even today.
For decades, it was the cosmic Holy Grail. The model accurately predicted the temperature
fluctuations of the leftover heat from the Big Bang, known as the Cosmic Microwave Background,
or CMB. It also serves as a handy explainer for the cosmic web of galaxies, clusters,
and voids that make up the known universe. It was hailed as a masterpiece.
But it has its flaws. It states that “baryonic matter”
matter, which is every single star, planet, moon, the air we breathe and our existence,
accounts for just 5% of the entire universe. The other 95% is divided into 2 distinct
categories, 2 invisible ghosts: Cold Dark Matter, which accounts for around 27% and
Dark Energy, which makes up the remaining 68%. Cold Dark Matter is a shadow material holding
galaxies together. Dark energy is the force driving the rapid expansion of the universe,
ripping the fabric of space apart. At least, that’s the theory.
In reality, despite decades of searching neither Cold Dark Matter nor Dark Energy has ever been
detected or identified in any physical form. So, the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model relies on
the assumption that 95% of the universe is made up of two things that are impossible to prove exist.
For decades, the theory was accepted, not because it made sense… but because
the technology to prove it wrong didn’t exist. Astronomers needed to go back 13.8 billion years,
to the dawn of time. Even the best deep-space telescopes weren’t strong enough. The ancient
light from the earliest days of the universe was out of reach. So the theory remained unchallenged.
At least until the next-generation space observation technologies were developed.
Then everything changed. But before we go any further,

According to the Lambda CDM model, after the Big Bang, there was a period of rapid expansion,
then a period of cooling. After 380,000 years, the universe transitioned into
the so-called “cosmic dark ages.” For tens of millions of years,
the universe was a ghost town. No stars. No galaxies. Nothing. It was just a primordial
mixture of gases drifting across space. Gravity then supposedly pulled these gases
into pockets of dark matter. It took millions of years to create the first
generation of primitive star formations. And it took billions of years to build mature galaxies.
But when scientists took a closer look at the deepest stretches of space,
they uncovered something that absolutely shattered the pre-existing timeline.
Instead of the dark and sparse space soup they expected, they found fully formed galaxies. They
had complex structures, orderly rotations, and high concentrations of heavy elements
that simply couldn’t exist at the start of space. Complex and mature galaxies shouldn’t be able to
exist without hundreds of millions of years of history behind them.
Faced with an impossible timeline, a broken “Zero Hour” and a missing 95% “dark sector,”
cosmology is now facing up to a frightening new reality. It’s a reality that forces them
to throw out everything they thought they knew about the known universe.
What if it didn’t explode out of an infinitely dense point of absolute nothingness, after all?
What if, instead, there was a different explanation?
There is an alternative. One built on absolute and verifiable facts.
And it’s called the Black Hole Universe. According to this model, the universe wasn’t
crushed into a zero-volume point, and it wasn’t born out of nowhere. Instead, we’re living inside
a gigantic black hole, which exists within a far larger, pre-existing “parent universe.”
What we call the Big Bang wasn’t the origin story of space and time.
It was, in fact, a “Big Bounce.” A massive quantum rebound occurring
safely inside a black hole’s event horizon. Imagine a colossal cloud of matter collapsing
under its own gravity in the parent universe, birthing a black hole. As matter was sucked in,
it compressed to extreme densities. Right before it could form a broken point of
singularity, it hit a quantum wall. The physical properties inverted.
Instead of collapsing, the matter violently rebounded into a brand new part of space.
What we see in the night sky is just the echo of that rebound.
We aren’t the product of an explosion that happened “out of nowhere,” we’re just part of
a potentially endless cosmic cycle. Our whole universe is a mere speck in a far larger one.
This isn’t just the random ramblings of theoretical physicists searching for some
alternative explanation to the Big Bang. It’s a framework that’s based on actual
data captured at the edge of observable space. That’s where the James Webb Space Telescope,
or JWST comes in. Its Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument scoured deep space and
locked onto a galaxy named JADES-GS-z14-0. This galaxy has a red-shift of about 14.18,
which means that it’s one of the most distant galaxies ever discovered.
The galaxy formed around 13.5 billion years ago, or around 300 million years after the Big Bang.
According to the Lambda Cold Dark Matter framework, space at that time should
have been empty, aside from primordial gas clouds swirling around dark matter pockets.
It certainly shouldn’t have contained any complex, fully-formed galaxies.
JADES-GS-z14-0 measures up at more than 1,600 light years wide and is packed with millions
of stars. But the real smoking gun was the spectroscopic analysis, which found signatures
of heavy elements, including ionized oxygen. This goes against the Cold Dark Matter model.
That says that hydrogen and helium might be present around the time this
galaxy formed. But oxygen can only appear after generations of stars being born, fusing, dying.
It’s the galaxy that shouldn’t exist. And that’s just the start.
For years, astrophysicists have been haunted by the “Hubble Tension”.
When scientists calculate how fast the universe expands using background radiation from the dawn
of time, they find a rapid expansion rate of about 67 to 68 kilometers per second per megaparsec. A
megaparsec is almost 3.3 million light years. But, when they look at the expansion rate
closer to home, that expansion jumps to 73 to 74 kilometers per second per megaparsec.
In physics, this is known as a “5-sigma statistical discrepancy”.
That means that there’s roughly a 1-in-3.5-million chance that this mismatch is a random fluke.
The equipment is perfect. The numbers are flawless. The mechanics are precise. Yet the
numbers refuse to play ball. It defies all logic.
The Big Bang framework is failing in two major ways:
it can’t explain how complex galaxies could have formed at the so-called “dawn of time.”
And it can't explain how the universe is expanding at two different speeds.
And if the theory is so broken, we have no other option but to find a more reliable alternative.
But modern physicists realized that they didn’t necessarily need to “throw out”
all the hard work that had been done by their predecessors. They just needed to modify it.
When Albert Einstein formulated his theory of General Relativity, he assumed that space-time
was able to curve, but wasn’t able to twist. Or, in more technical terms, it didn’t possess any
“intrinsic torsion.” It meant that a collapsing star was always destined to compress into an
infinitely dense point… a singularity. But what if space-time can twist?
TheEinstein-Cartan-Sciama-Kibble, or ECSK theory proves that when matter collapses to
its extreme lime, the spin density skyrockets, generating an enormous torsional field. It
acts like a giant cosmic shock absorber. At that moment, gravity essentially inverts,
going from powerfully attractive to fiercely repulsive in an instant. That’s
what triggers the resulting “Big Bounce” effect. This theory says that the universe didn’t just
explode into existence out of nowhere. Instead, the mass of the universe compressed into a tiny
point before violently bouncing back. It was a continuous event happening
inside a black hole. Several scientists have
explored this idea dating back to the 1970s. But today, it’s Polish theoretical physicist, Dr.
Nikodem Poplawski, who is leading the charge. He argues that the Black Hole Universe model removes
one of the biggest barriers to human exploration and understanding of the known universe…
The illusion of Time Zero. For decades, the classic
Big Bang model forced that on us. It claimed that space and time exploded
out of nothingness at the point when “time equals zero,” rendering any discussion of what might have
happened before that point moot. Stephen Hawking once said that even asking the question “What
happened before the Big Bang?” was pointless, like asking “What is north of the North Pole?”
And it was this dogmatic viewpoint that protected a broken equation for so many years.
The word “singularity” did all of the heavy-lifting, but was completely mysterious,
defying so many of the laws of classical physics. Replacing that singularity with a quantum
“bounce” changes everything. It means that time no longer
started at “Time Zero”. Instead, it flowed continuously before the bounce,
roared through it, and carried its momentum and energy into the creation of our universe.
According to Poplawski, the singularity wasn’t the start of reality. It was just the wall that
previous generations of physicists couldn’t get past. They didn’t have the tools, knowledge,
and data they needed to break through Now, they do.
And the rule of cause and effect has been restored.
In the process, the classic Big Bang problems have been solved. The classical theory struggled
to explain why the universe started off in such a low entropy state. The Big Bounce model solves
that by revealing that the low entropy was a natural consequence of space-time torsion.
The classical theory also had no answers for the so-called “Horizon Problem.” This is the
mystery of why regions at different ends of the universe share the same temperature,
despite being so far apart. The Big Bounce framework fixes that,
too. It explains that those parts of space were causally connected before
the bounce occurred. It would explain why they share the same thermal characteristics.
And, the classical theory ultimately rested on an “ex nihilo” mystery of something coming from
nothing. But the Big Bounce replaces that with a much more comprehensible “something
came from something” explanation. If you expand the theory further,
an extraordinary realization emerges. If our universe was birthed from the
gravitational collapse of a dying star in a parent universe, couldn’t the exact same thing happen
again and again in other black holes? Scientists estimate that there are 40
quintillion black holes in our universe. When we apply Einstein-Cartan-Sciama-Kibble
theory across them all, it’s possible that each one could house its very own separate universe.
Inside those universes could be countless more black holes, with their own universes,
and the pattern could continue like that, infinitely. It aligns perfectly with the
“Multiverse” theory. Our entire universe is just one of an infinite number of bubble universes. An
endless fractal where every possibility plays out an infinite number of times. It leaves us
with infinite worlds identical to our own and countless more changing in ways we can’t imagine.
This completely transforms our picture of reality even further.
It suggests that our universe isn’t that special at all.
It’s an infinitely small piece of an infinitely larger entity.
A tiny speck among countless others. If the parent and child universe concept
is accurate, then there’s no telling how far back that chain could go. Our universe could
be sat inside a parent, which is, itself, sat inside another parent, and so on.
And just as real children inherit characteristics from their birth parents, child universes are also
believed to inherit certain features from their parents. Features like the strength of gravity,
the speed of light, and even the size and mass of individual particles. Everything is
passed down from parent to child, albeit slightly altered each time due to the quantum fluctuations
that occur during every single “Big Bounce.” It’s almost like the process of evolution,
expanded on a cosmic scale. Universes with the right kinds of
physical constraints are able to form vast numbers of massive stars, dense galaxies, and black
holes. They go on to give birth to countless more universes of their own, forming family trees that
get infinitely wider as they grow. Our universe was just one that happened to have formed from
the right kind of parent, with sufficient stars, heavy elements, and other key characteristics.
This is the next step in understanding our universe.
We’re taking the next step forward, acknowledging that our universe isn’t
actually some sort of unique arena of existence. It’s a singular node in a far larger network.
And the facts that physicists may have been wrong up to now or that they continue to disagree on
matters like the Hubble Tension and “95% Dark Sector” aren’t signs that science has failed.
They’re signs that it’s progressing. That our understanding of everything around us is evolving,
and that evolution may involve having to cross-out or rewrite some of our
old notes and theories to bring them up to date. That’s exactly what scientists
and astronomers have been doing for centuries. And so, when we glance deep into the night sky
using the most advanced telescopes on Earth, it turns out we probably aren’t looking at
the “dawn of the cosmos,” after all. Just the dawn of our little pocket of
it. The aftermath of a chaotic cosmic rebound in a reality that is infinitely older, larger, and more
interconnected than we could ever have imagined. Think you know everything there is about space?
